strengths: Rigorous theoretical framework: Novel generalization from KL divergence to arbitrary f-divergences with sound mathematical foundation. Section 4.1's gradient analysis and Section 4.2's convergence analysis using dynamical systems theory are sophisticated and provide actionable insights (e.g., Eq. 106 relating 1/f''(1) to convergence speed).

Comprehensive technical approach: Provides both closed-form solutions for specific divergences and variational formulation for arbitrary f-divergences. Systematically treats multiple divergences and shows prior work (CAbl, DoCo) as special cases.

Strong experimental validation: Extensive evaluation across multiple concepts, iteration counts (500, 2000, 5000), and anchor strategies. Figure 2 effectively validates theoretical gradient predictions. Multi-concept sequential erasure demonstrates scalability. Honest reporting of trade-offs.

Well-executed presentation: Clear motivation, good visual aids, thorough related work positioning, and comprehensive appendices supporting reproducibility. Paper is well-organized despite technical complexity.
Practical contribution to important problem: Addresses real safety concerns in diffusion models (NSFW removal, copyright protection). Framework is general and could extend to other generative models.
weaknesses: Limited practical advantages: Empirical improvements of H² over MSE are marginal and inconsistent (Tables 3-5 show H² sometimes wins on quality preservation, sometimes loses on erasure metrics). Differences often fall within noise for CS/CA metrics, undermining claims of superiority.

Lack of practical guidance: Paper provides no clear operational guidance on which divergence to use when. Theorem 4.2 predicts H² and JS should be faster, but all variants converge within 500 steps empirically, raising questions about practical relevance of convergence bounds.

Theoretical limitations not fully addressed: (1) Only local convergence guarantees (Theorem 4.2); global convergence unknown. (2) Claim that different f-divergences yield same optimal solution (Eq. 3) needs formal justification, especially given mode-seeking vs mode-covering differences discussed later. (3) Assumptions B.6-B.8 are strong and unverified empirically.

Incomplete experimental evaluation: (1) Limited baselines—only MSE and CAbl compared; missing DoCo, AGE, RECELER despite mentioning them. (2) Single model version (SD v1.4) limits generalizability claims. (3) No robustness evaluation: can unlearned concepts be recovered via adversarial prompts or fine-tuning? (4) No human evaluation of visual quality; CLIP metrics have known biases.

Key experimental ambiguities: (1) KID metric interpretation is subjective and contentious—higher KID for erased concepts could indicate either successful destruction or collateral damage. (2) Regularization effects (prior preservation, gradient surgery) appear critical but no principled selection strategy provided across 9 variants tested.
